## Results

IF targets METTL3 to modulate TGF-β signalisng pathway and improve outcomes in TP53-driven glioma
Utilizing a computational approach to quantify DR-related molecular activities13, previous analysis of patient data from TCGA indicates that DR-related therapeutic targets hold significant potential for the treatment of GBM. We applied this method separately to CDKN2A subtype and TP53 subtype GBM, and observed that TP53 GBM patients exhibit higher DR scores compared to CDKN2A group patients, indicating that TP53 group GBM are more susceptible to the effects of DR (Fig. 1a). Then, we developed Cdkn2a and Tp53 GBM mouse models, respectively recapitulating the human CDKN2A subtype and TP53 subtype (See the “Methods” section for details). For Cdkn2a and Tp53 GBM mouse models, we randomly divided the mice into IF and ad libitum (AL) diet groups for different intervention (Fig. 1b). Experimental findings indicated that IF did not confer benefits to Cdkn2a GBM mice (Fig. 1c). Conversely, mice with Tp53 GBM in the IF group exhibited a markedly improved prognosis compared to those in the AL group (Fig. 1d), consistent with the conclusion of previous studies that IF contributes to the prognosis of GBM7. The results of hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining indicated that in Tp53 GBM model, there was a downward trend in tumor size, but a lack thereof in the Cdkn2a GBM model (Fig. 1e, f and Supplementary Fig. 1).

Subsequently, differentially expressed genes (DEGs) analysis of bulk transcriptomics on Tp53 GBM mice revealed 1443 up-regulated genes and 1952 down-regulated genes in the Tp53-IF group, compared to the Tp53-AL group (Fig. 1g). Notably, Mettl3, a well-known RNA-binding protein that regulates RNA methylation, was one of the down-regulated genes (Fig. 1g). Moreover, KEGG analysis revealed that these DEGs were enriched in several tumor-related pathways, such as the TGF-β signaling pathway, MAPK signaling pathway, and proteoglycans in cancer, among others (Fig. 1h). Notably TGF-β is widely acknowledged as a core pathway in tumor progression, with studies demonstrating that inhibition of TGFB2 can suppress GBM22. Enrichment analysis of differential gene sets between CDKN2A and TP53 GBM patients, revealed that the TGF-β signaling pathway was significantly altered between CDKN2A and TP53 groups, suggesting differential activation of TGF-β signaling in patients with Tp53 versus Cdkn2a subtypes (Supplementary Fig. 2a, b). And Tgfb2 is core regulator in TGF-β pathway situated upstream in cancer23 (Supplementary Fig. 3b). Furthermore, differential analysis between Tp53-IF and Cdkn2a-IF groups revealed a significant decrease of Mettl3 in Tp53-IF group (Supplementary Fig. 3c). Enrichment analysis further demonstrated significant involvement of the TGF-β signaling pathway among the DEGs (Supplementary Fig. 3d, e), suggesting that Cdkn2a and Tp53 GBM model respond differently to the METTL3-mediated TGF-β signaling pathway.

Moreover, we analyzed human transcriptomic data from 41 individuals following IF and controls (GEO DataSets: GSE196335)24. We observed significant enrichment of DEGs related to tumor pathways, notably the TGF-β pathway (Supplementary Fig. 3f). Subsequently, molecular functional analysis of gene ontology (GO) of DEGs revealed significant enrichment in protein binding, nucleotide binding, and RNA binding (Fig. 1i). Additionally, given previous reports indicating that inhibiting METTL3 can suppress GBM25. Network analysis revealed METTL3 as a key hub gene among these DEGs (Supplementary Fig. 3g), suggesting that IF induces alterations in pivotal pathways like METTL3 and TGF-β at the population level.

Further investigation of the Chinese Glioma Genome Atlas database26 unveiled a notable correlation between the expression of TGFB2 and METTL3 (Fig. 1j)26. Inhibiting METTL3 led to the downregulation of TGFB2 (Fig. 1k, Supplementary Fig. 3h–j), indicating that downregulation of METTL3 inhibits TGFB2 expression. Furthermore, it was reported that m6A modification of TGFB2 contributes to GBM pathogenesis25, and TGF-β signaling pathway regulating by METTL3 is associated with tumor development27. Our findings suggest that IF regulates RNA binding protein METTL3, which may serve as crucial downstream regulatory mechanisms of IF.

The interplay between m6A and transcriptomic landscapes modulated by IF in GBM from single-cell and bulk analyses
METTL3 generally regulates downstream genes like TGFB2 through m6A27. Therefore, we performed m6A-seq on GBM tissues from both the Tp53-AL and Tp53-IF groups of GBM mice, and found slightly different m6A motifs between the Tp53-AL group and the Tp53-IF group (Fig. 2a). Our analysis also revealed a decreased number of m6A modifications in the Tp53-IF group (Fig. 2b), suggesting that Tp53-IF may inhibit m6A modification. Furthermore, these modification sites were typically found in regions related to gene expression regulation (Fig. 2c). Additionally, a notable reduction in m6A modification on Tgfb2 was observed in the Tp53-IF group compared to the Tp53-AL group, as depicted in the tracks (Fig. 2d). We found that these significantly altered m6A sites are enriched with the Mettl3 binding motif28, further confirming the reported role of Mettl3 in regulating Tgfb2 and downstream genes (Fig. 2d). Even though the association between the METTL3-TGF-β pathway and tumor development has been previously reported27, our findings provide further evidence that Mettl3 may bind to Tgfb2 and that IF induces a decrease in m6A abundance on Tgfb2.

To precisely determine the single-cell level atlas under the influence of IF, we conducted scRNA-seq on GBM tissues from Tp53 GBM mice in both the AL and IF groups. We visualized 64,918 cells using Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP) and identified 37 clusters (Supplementary Fig. 4a). Subsequently, we identified 20 major cell populations in the GBM tissues of GBM mice from both the Tp53-AL and Tp53-IF groups (Fig. 2e, f). The clusters were manually annotated with their respective cellular identities using highly expressed genes and cell-specific markers from each cluster (Fig. 2g, Supplementary Fig. 4b, Supplementary Table 1, methods). According to single-cell transcriptomic profiling of the whole mouse brain29, the cell populations can be divided into excitatory neurons, inhibitory neurons, medium spiny neurons, tumor cells, oligodendrocytes, endothelial cells, microglia and macrophages. Excitatory neurons included ExN−L2/3−IT, ExN−L5−IT, ExN−L5−ET, ExN−Olf, ExN−L6−CT, and ExN−L5/6−NP; inhibitory neurons included InN−Chat, InN−Sst, InN−Syt6, InN−Olf, InN−Adarb2, and InN−Lhx6; medium spiny neurons included MSN−D1 and MSN−D2; tumor cells included OPC−like, AC−like, and MES−like (Fig. 2h).

Pseudotime analysis indicated that AL- and IF-treated tumor cells were distributed across the two branches of the trajectory (Fig. 2i, Supplementary Fig. 4c). Moreover, IF-treated tumor cells in elderly individuals were projected at the end of one branch along the developmental trajectory, suggesting that these cells were in the terminal differentiated state in elderly individuals (Fig. 2i). Additionally, expression patterns of Mettl3 and Tgfb2 in tumor cells were observed gradually changing from AL to IF (Fig. 2i). This suggested again that IF was associated with the downregulation of Mettl3 and Tgfb2 expression in Tp53 GBM tumor cells. Employing our single-cell m6A (scm6A) detection method30, we assessed the m6A abundance in single cell level of two groups (Fig. 2j). Our findings revealed a decrease in m6A abundance in cells from the Tp53-IF group. (Fig. 2k). Once again, we elucidated the regulatory profile of m6A and TGF-β signaling pathway at the single-cell level.

IF regulates methionine metabolism influencing m6A-regulated genes in brain regional heterogeneity using spatial omics data
It is well known that fasting primarily affects metabolites. Herein, we conducted metabolomic analysis of blood samples from Tp53 GBM mice of both the AL and IF groups. We found distinct metabolic profiles between the Tp53-IF and Tp53-AL groups (Supplementary Fig. 5a), with the majority of metabolites showing significant downregulation in the Tp53-IF group compared to the Tp53-AL groups (Fig. 3a), notably methionine and S-adenosylmethionine (SAM) (Fig. 3b). Furthermore, differential metabolites could be enriched in methionine metabolism-related pathways (Fig. 3c). Methionine and SAM serve as the substrate for m6A, thus the reduction in methionine and SAM caused by IF results in decreased m6A levels18,31. Consequently, this SAM-mediated m6A modification downregulates the TGF-β signaling pathway, thereby inhibiting GBM. Additionally, supplementation with methionine has been reported to raise SAM levels in various regions of the central nervous system32. These results indicated that the reduction in methionine caused by IF can inhibit the TGF-β pathway through the regulation of SAM-m6A axis.

To further investigate the correlation between gene expression and metabolism in different spatial regions of the whole brain, we conducted spatial metabolomic and spatial transcriptomic sequencing on samples from Tp53 GBM models treated with AL and IF. The Tp53-IF group and the Tp53-AL group exhibited distinct spatial metabolic profiles across the whole brain (Supplementary Fig. 5b, c), and within the same sample, different brain regions, including tumor sites, also displayed distinct metabolic characteristics (Fig. 3d). In Fig. 3e, the results showed that the tumor region in the Tp53-AL group was enriched with SAM, while the tumor region in the Tp53-IF group has lower SAM content. Additionally, spatial transcriptomic data also show higher expression levels of Mettl3 and Tgfb2 in the tumor region of the Tp53-AL group compared to the tumor region of the Tp53-IF group (Fig. 3f, Supplementary Fig. 5d). Furthermore, the Tp53 GBM tissues from the IF and AL groups exhibit distinct spatial transcriptomic characteristics across different regions (Supplementary Fig. 5e). We conducted an integrated analysis of spatial metabolomic data and spatial transcriptomic data to investigate the differences between the Tp53-IF group and the Tp53-AL group (Fig. 3g). According to differential gene expression features in different regions, the differential genes in spatial transcriptomic data were divided into 24 clusters, enriched in different brain regions (Fig. 3g, h). Similarly, based on the differential metabolite features between different regions of Tp53-AL and Tp53-IF, all differential metabolites were clustered into 17 clusters, with each cluster enriched in different regions possessing distinct differential metabolite characteristics (Fig. 3g, i). We found significant difference of enrichment of SAM, Mettl3, and Tgfb2 in the tumor region (Fig. 3g), indicating that the SAM-METTL3-TGF-β pathway plays an important role in IF.

The gut microbiota, modulated by IF, regulates methionine levels to regulate m6A modification
Given that the overall food intake during our breeding was essentially the same, with the only distinction being the feeding pattern, we posit that this metabolic disparity is not attributed to dietary intake but rather to other factors. Methionine is an essential amino acid that cannot be synthesized in the body; however, it can be extensively produced by intestinal bacteria33,34. Thus, we conducted metagenomic analysis of feces from Tp53 and Cdkn2a GBM mice of both AL and IF groups, aiming to explore why IF would cause a decrease of methionine levels. We found significant differences in the gut microbiota between the IF and AL groups of Tp53 and Cdkn2a GBM mice (Fig. 4a, Supplementary Fig. 6a). To be specific, we found that bacteroidota (phylum level) and bacteroidia (class level) seemed to be more abundant in the AL group at the levels of phylum and class (Fig. 4b, c, Supplementary Fig. 6b, c). Then, we applied linear discriminant analysis (LDA) effect size (LEfSe) method to explore the differences in bacterial taxa composition between IF and AL group of Tp53 and Cdkn2a GBM mice. Our results showed that Tp53-IF mice had a decreased abundance of g.Alistipes, s.Prevotella sp. CAG:873, etc. (Fig. 4d), while families Rikenellaceae and Eggerthellaceae were identified as major contributors to the gut microbiota in the Tp53-AL group compared to the Tp53-IF group (Supplementary Fig. 6d). In addition, LDA of Cdkn2a-AL group and Cdkn2a-IF also revealed that s__Alistipes ihumii was significantly abundance in AL (Supplementary Fig. 6e). It is worth noting that many bacteria involved in methionine synthesis are at the genus level of Alistipes35, which belong to f. Rikenellaceae, such as ihumii, montrealensis, communis, senegalensis. And Prevotella sp. CAG:873 also has the function of synthesizing methionine36 (https://www.uniprot.org/uniprotkb/R7J0K0/entry). We conducted differential analysis of gut microbiota abundant between IF and AL groups on Tp53 GBM mice and used MetOrigin37 to annotate these various microbial metabolites and their metabolic functions. We found that the microbiota related to methionine synthesis were all down regulated in Tp53-IF group (Fig. 4e). Furthermore, KEGG enrichment analysis suggested that the significantly differential metabolites were mainly involved in the cancer related pathways, Ras signaling pathway, glioma pathway and Cysteine and methionine metabolism (Fig. 4f). We also annotated the differentially represented metagenomic data using eggNOG and identified significant associations with methionine metabolism (Supplementary Fig. 6f). We conducted a correlation analysis between the abundance of microbial communities, which associated with methionine synthesis, and the abundance of differentially present metabolites across all samples. This analysis revealed significant correlations between many differential metabolites and microbial communities, including methionine (Fig. 4g, h). The relative abundances for methionine-producing bacteria were tracked across multiple time points in both Cdkn2a-IF and Tp53-IF groups. The results reveal dynamic temporal changes and further support the association between these taxa and IF response in Tp53-mutant GBM (Supplementary Fig. 7). Overall, the downregulation of methionine is explained to be regulated by the gut microbiota restructured by IF, as previous studies have shown that IF can decrease methionine levels through microbiota16.

Validation of IF’s GBM inhibition via microbiota-methionine-m6A-Tgfb2 axis
To further validate our conclusions, we injected mice intracranially with shRAS/shp53 and dual luciferase-GFP expression vectors. These mice consistently developed large, invasive tumor masses, which were confirmed through bioluminescence imaging (Fig. 5a). The Tp53 GBM mice were divided into nine groups: the Tp53-AL group, the Tp53-IF group, the Tp53-AL group treated with STM2457 (METTL3 inhibitor) (Tp53-STM2457-AL), the Tp53-AL group subjected to fecal microbiota transplant from IF mice (Tp53-FMT-AL), the Tp53-IF group with Mettl3 gene over-expression (Tp53-M3OE-AL), the Tp53-IF group with enhanced methionine intake (Tp53-MET-IF), and the Tp53-IF group injected with entacapone (Tp53-ENT-IF), an FTO inhibitor aimed at enhancing m6A modifications, the Tp53-AL group with broad-spectrum antibiotics (Tp53-ABX-AL), the Tp53-IF group with broad-spectrum antibiotics (Tp53-ABX-IF). The Cdkn2a GBM mice were divided into six groups: the Cdkn2a-AL group, the Cdkn2a-IF group, the Cdkn2a-AL group treated with STM2457 (Cdkn2a-STM2457-AL), the Cdkn2a-AL group subjected to fecal microbiota transplant from Cdkn2a-IF mice (Cdkn2a-FMT-AL), the Cdkn2a-AL group with broad-spectrum antibiotics (Cdkn2a-ABX-AL), the Cdkn2a-IF group with broad-spectrum antibiotics (Cdkn2a-ABX-IF). The results demonstrated that both IF, METTL3 inhibition even AL (Tp53-STM2457-AL), and the alteration of microbiota associated with IF (Tp53-FMT-AL) in Tp53 GBM mice groups slowed tumor growth (Fig. 5a–c) and significantly improved prognosis (Fig. 5d), but no significance in microbiota-inhibition groups (Tp53-ABX-AL and Tp53-ABX-IF) and IF-non-response groups (Cdkn2a-) (Supplementary Figs. 8a–e, h–k, 9c–e), indicating that IF inhibits Tp53 subtype GBM progression via the gut microbiota and METTL3. Concurrently, we observed significant reductions in the abundance of bacteria involved in methionine synthesis (Supplementary Fig. 8f), SAM and methionine levels in feces and serum (Fig. 5e–h), m6A levels (Fig. 5i), and protein levels of TGFB2 and METTL3 (Fig. 5j–l). These results further validated that IF can downregulate methionine, m6A, and TGFB2.

However, augmenting methionine intake or increasing m6A levels in mice from the Tp53-IF group led to tumor sizes and prognosis comparable to those of the Tp53-AL group (Fig. 5a–d), suggesting the inhibitory effects of IF can be reversed by replenishing methionine or m6A levels, further indicating that methionine and m6A are the principal mechanisms through which IF influences GBM. The abundance of bacterium ihumii in the Tp53-IF group, Tp53-FMT-AL group, Tp53-MET-IF group, and Tp53-ENT-IF group significantly decreased compared to the Tp53-AL group, indicating that the abundance of bacterium ihumii is regulated by IF (Fig. 5d). Moreover, we further discovered that the Tp53-IF Group, Tp53-FMT-AL group, Tp53-MET-IF group, and Tp53-ENT-IF group exhibited analogous overall gut microbiota profiles (Supplementary Fig. 8g). Meanwhile, the abundance of SAM and methionine was regulated by IF and IF fecal microbiota in both Tp53 and Cdkn2a subtype GBM (Fig. 5e–h, Supplementary Fig. 8h–k), suggesting that IF-regulated gut microbiota suppresses methionine. The decrease in m6A levels caused by IF or IF fecal microbiota suppression in Tp53 GBM mice, can be restored by methionine and FTO inhibitors (Fig. 5i). But in microbiota-inhibition groups (Tp53-ABX-AL and Tp53-ABX-IF) and IF-non-response groups (Cdkn2a-AL and Cdkn2a-IF), there was no significance for m6A levels (Supplementary Fig. 9a, b). These results further highlighting the reliability of the IF-gut microbiota-methionine-m6A signaling axis. Additionally, Western blot results demonstrated that the m6A suppressed by IF or FMT ultimately regulated the protein level of TGFB2 and the entire TGF-β signaling pathway (Fig. 5j–m). Overall, the results indicated that the biological effect of IF depends on m6A, which is the downstream of the gut microbiota-methionine pathway.

## Methods

This study protocol, including the use of mice, was reviewed and approved by the Institutional Review Board of Guangxi Medical University (Ethics: 202307007).

RNA-sequencing analysis
Fresh tissue was processed using Qiagen RNALipid Tissue Kit. Quality of the RNA was determined using TapeStation. The sequencing strategy was paired-end 150 bp for NovaSeq 6000. The raw sequence reads have been stored at Genome Sequence Archive (GSA: https://bigd.big.ac.cn/gsub/) (Accession Number: CRA015912). We used FastQC package (https://www.bioinformatics.babraham.ac.uk/projects/fastqc/) (v0.11.9) to perform the sequencing quality control, and reads were aligned to the mouse reference genome (mm10) using Hisat249 (v2.2.1) with default parameters. Then, StringTie50 (v1.3.3b) was used for assembly and quantification of counts matrix and TPM (transcripts per kilobase of exon model per million mapped reads) of each annotated gene.

We used DESeq251 (v1.42.0) to detect significantly DEGs, with a threshold of |log fold change (FC)|>1.2 and a Benjamini-Hochberg corrected P<0.01. Subsequently, we utilized DAVID52 (https://david.ncifcrf.gov/) for KEGG enrichment analysis to identify significantly enriched pathways.

The population RNA-seq data of the AL and IF groups were obtained from Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/) (Accession Number: GSE196335)24. We identified DEGs and performed Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA) by Hallmark database and Gene Ontology (GO) enrichment analysis by DAVID database. Then, DEGs were used to construct PPI network through GeneMANIA web tools53,54, and all parameters were set to default values.

m6A-sequencing analysis
Likewise, m6A-sequencing was performed on two groups of Tp53 GBM mice tissues, and the raw data were available through GSA (Accession Number: CRA015927). The reads were mapped to mouse reference genome (mm10) using Hisat249 (v2.2.1). The resulting BAM files were used for peak calling and differential Peak analysis with the R package exomePeak255 (v1.14.3). In order to explore the characteristics of m6A, motif enrichment analysis was conducted using HOMER software56, by RNA backgrounds with randomly permutated sequences (HOMER parameter: line=1000, size=200). Then, distributions of m6A peaks were plotted by the R package Guitar (v2.18.0), using mm10 as referenced sequence57, and all parameters were default. We employed bamCoverage to generate coverage tracks in bigWig format, using mm10 as the reference genome. We then analyzed Tgfb2 read coverage and Mettl3 binding motifs in m6A-seq data from Tp53-AL and Tp53-IF groups, using IGV58 (v2.8.13) as the visualization tool.

Single-cell transcriptome analysis
We performed single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) of Tp53 GBM mice tissue of AL and IF groups, with raw data available through GSA (Accession Number: CRA016372). Data alignment and gene quantification were conducted using the official 10X Genomics CellRanger (v5.0.0) platform after sequencing. Based on the quantification results provided by CellRanger, a secondary screening and cell quality control were performed using Seurat59 (v5.0.2), adhering to the following criteria: (1) nCounts < 50,000; (2) nFeature > 500 and nFeature < 7000; (3) Mitochondrial gene proportion < 1%; (4) Red-blood-cell gene proportion < 1%. Then, the selected cells were processed by batch effect inspection, normalization and clustering (nFeature: 3000, dims: 1/20, resolution: 0.5, other parameters were default). UMAP60 were used to visualize. And, characteristic genes were used to define each cell type (Supplementary Table 1).

Monocle2 (v2.24.0) was utilized for pseudotime-based ordering of tumor cells, followed by visualization using the UMAP method. Subsequently, estimation of cell size factors and dispersions was conducted. Utilizing the top 10 DEGs, the cellular trajectory was delineated, employing the setOrderingFilter function for standardization. After that, dimensionality reduction was performed using the DDRTree method. In addition, cells were ordered and depicted along a pseudotime trajectory using the orderCells function to accurately represent the developmental dynamics of the cells. Finally, we used scm6A30 (v1.0) with default parameters to predict m6A abundance at the single-cell level for all cells and conducted statistical analysis on cells in the AL and IF groups using T-tests.

Spatial transcriptomics analysis
The tissues were obtained from Tp53 GBM mice after resection, fixed by formalin, and embedded in paraffin. After RNA quality control (DV200 > 30%), 5-micron thick sections were mounted onto Visium Gene Expression slides. The samples were stained with H&E and stained slides were scanned under a microscope, followed by decrosslinking using 0.1 N HCl and TE Buffer (pH 9.0) to release RNA. Three pairs of specific probes (5′ containing Small RNA Read 2S and 3′ containing poly-A) were used for probe hybridization overnight. After hybridization, the cDNA libraries were constructed according to the 10X protocol, and sequencing was performed on NovaSeq 6000 (Illumina). Raw imaging data were processed using SCiLS Lab software, applying smoothing and RMS normalization to adjust peak intensities66. A average mass spectra were derived from selected tissue regions, plotting m/z ratios against the RMS-normalized average peak intensities. Prominent peaks were subjected to MS/MS analysis, and the resulting spectra were matched against databases for identification. Low-intensity peaks were searched in databases within a 10 ppm mass accuracy. Utilizing the data gleaned from substance identification, we engaged in spatially-aware nearest shrunk centroids clustering to delineate regional information based on all targeted peaks67,68. The spatial mapping of identified peaks was executed to visualize the distribution of substances across the tissue microenvironment. Prior to clustering, the dataset underwent z-score normalization to standardize inter-sample variability. Subsequently, a hierarchical clustering heatmap analysis was conducted on the entire sample collection, employing the ComplexHeatmap (v2.20.0) application for sophisticated visualization of the metabolite distribution patterns69. Data were available in OMIX database (Accession Number: OMIX012365).

Metabolomics analysis
For each group of Tp53 and Cdkn2a GBM mice, we selected blood and feces samples for metabolomic sequencing. Fecal samples were collected at multiple time points, including before the initiation of fasting, during fasting (15 days), and at the terminal stage (30 days) of the experiment. In contrast, brain tissues and blood samples were harvested only at the terminal stage. After homogenizing and incubation on ice, the samples were centrifuged and injected into the LC-MS/MS system for analysis62. The mobile phases consisted of eluent, with a gradient profile optimized for comprehensive metabolite coverage. The mass spectrometer was operated in both positive and negative polarity modes.

Raw data were available in MassIVE database (Accession Number: MSV000100119), and were processed using Compound Discoverer 3.3 (Thermo Fisher Scientific) for peak alignment, picking, and quantitation. Data were normalized against total spectral intensity. Molecular formulas were predicted, and peaks were matched against databases like mzCloud and mzVault for qualitative and quantitative results. Then, these metabolites were annotated using the KEGG, HMDB, and LIPIDMaps databases. Principal Component Analysis and Partial Least Squares Discriminant Analysis (PLS-DA) were conducted using metaX63. Univariate analysis (t-test) was employed to calculate statistical significance (P values). Metabolites with variable importance in prediction (VIP) > 1, P < 0.05 and |log FC| > 1 were considered differentially expressed metabolites64. For cluster heatmaps, data were standardized by the z-scores of the intensity areas of differential metabolites and plotted using the pheatmap (v1.0.12) package in R (v4.3.2). And, KEGG enrichment analysis for metabolites was performed by the MetaboAnalyst 6.0 online web65 (https://www.metaboanalyst.ca/).

Spatial metabolomics analysis
Tissues on Tp53 GBM mice were cryosectioned at 10µm thickness. Then, sections were transferred to prechilled ITO slides and warmed until transparent, followed by drying using friction on the slide’s reverse. 2,5-dihydroxybenzoic acid (DHB) matrix was sprayed onto the tissue sections using a TM-Sprayer. ITO slides were mounted on a mass spectrometer target plate, and tissue regions were outlined using DataImaging software. The tissue was scanned by a laser to induce ionization, and the released molecules were analyzed to obtain mass-to-charge ratio (m/z) and peak intensity data. Raw data were processed in SCiLS Lab software for smoothing and Root Mean Square (RMS) normalization, generating relative intensity values for m/z ratios, which were then visualized as pixels on an imaging heatmap.

Metagenomic sequencing and analysis
The feces of the mice were collected for subsequent testing. We constructed the DNA libraries by fragmenting DNA, end repair, adapter ligation, PCR amplification, and purification. Sequencing on the Illumina platform generated raw data, which was cleaned by deleting adapter contamination, low-quality bases (Q < 20) and removing human host DNA using the Bowtie2 software70,71. And, raw data was available in GSA (Accession Number: CRA015939). MEGAHIT software was used for assembly analysis of Clean Data72, then the clean data was aligned to the initial gene catalog by using Bowtie2 to calculate the number of reads of the genes on each sample alignment. Gene profiles were derived by mapping high-quality sequencing reads to a reference gene catalog. The relative abundance profiles of microbial communities were then inferred from the gene-level relative abundances.

The dissimilarities between two groups were analyzed by the nonredundant genes, and visually represented by the Bray-Curtis distances based principal coordinate analysis (PCoA). Metastats and LEfSe analysis73 (LDA Score is 4 by default) were conducted to identify species-level differences between groups. To elucidate the function of differential species, we performed functional enrichment analysis by KEGG74,75 (https://www.genome.jp/kegg/) and eggNOG76 (http://eggnog5.embl.de/#/app/home) databases. Subsequently, we identified 29 bacterial groups that synthesized methionine, and Pearson correlation analysis was used to calculate the correlation between bacterial groups and differential metabolites to further explore the function of bacterial groups.

Lentivirus construction
The study employed the methodology by utilizing lentiviruses carrying HrasG12V, sh-p53, or sh-cdkn2a/sh-cdkn2b to induce a GBM model2. To be specific, the lentiviral vector used to induce mouse GBM contained an HRASV12 fragment along with either a shp53 or shCDKN2A and shCDKN2B fragment. The co-expression of HRASV12 and luciferase was facilitated by Internal Ribosome Entry Site (IRES). The lentiviral vector is co-transfected with packaging plasmids pCMVΔ8.9 and pMD2.G into human embryonic kidney 293T cells. The supernatant containing lentiviral particles is collected and centrifuged at 4°C and 130,000 × g for 2.5 h. After centrifugation, the lentiviral particles are resuspended in phosphate-buffered saline containing 0.1% bovine serum albumin. Finally, the lentiviral particles are quantified using qPCR. All shRNA target sequences used in this study have been provided in Supplementary Table 2. These sequences were synthesized by BGI Genomics Co., Ltd. All plasmids, oligonucleotides, and viral vectors newly generated in this study are available from the corresponding author.

Animal models
The 7–8-week-old female C57BL/6J used in this study were sourced from Gempharmatech Co., Ltd (Jiangsu, China). The prepared lentivirus, as described in lentivirus construction section, was stereotactically injected into the hippocampus of the mice using a stereotaxic instrument. In summary, the anesthetized mice were secured with ear bars and a nose clamp. A 0.8 mm cranial drill bit was employed to thin the skull, following which 2 µL of purified lentivirus particles (1×109/mL) were drawn into a 5 µL syringe and administered at a rate of 1 µL/min. The injection was performed using specific coordinates: 1.6 mm lateral and 1.2 mm anterior to the bregma, and 1.75 mm below the skull surface. Post-injection, the needle remained in place for 3 min before being gradually withdrawn over a period of 1 min2. The procedure was concluded with suturing of the injection site on the mouse’s head. All procedures conducted in this research were approved by the animal ethics committee of the Guangxi Medical University (202307007), and all mice were maintained under pathogen-free conditions. According to our approved protocol, mice were monitored daily, and were euthanized immediately if they exhibited neurological deficits, persistent lethargy, reduced mobility, seizures.

Animal treatment and group
Mice were housed in a specific pathogen–free facility under a 12-h light/12-h dark cycle, with controlled ambient temperature (22 ± 2°C) and humidity (50–60%). Animals had free access to food and water unless specified otherwise in the experimental design. All animals were fed a standard rodent chow diet (Nanning Yancheng Biotechnology Co., Ltd, YC-6680). The diet composition was provided by the manufacturer and appropriate for standard laboratory rodent maintenance.

The GBM-bearing mice (Tp53 or Cdkn2a) were randomly divided into several experimental groups: For the control group (AL), mice were given ad libitum diet. For the Intermittent Fasting (IF) group, the mice underwent a fasting regimen where their food was removed for a 24-h period (Supplementary Fig. 3a). The total food intake was maintained at the same level across the groups, and the mice in this group had free access to water throughout the fasting period. For Tp53- and Cdkn2a-STM2457-AL mice, STM2457 (TargtMol, T9060) was dissolved in 20% (w/v) 2-hydroxyproply β-cyclodextrin vehicle (Sigma, H107). And then, indicated doses77 of STM2457 or vehicle were delivered to the mice via intraperitoneal injection on day 10 after injection of lentivirus, once daily for total 2 weeks (14 treatments). For the FMT (Cdkn2a- and Tp53-FMT-AL) group, A broad-spectrum antibiotic cocktail (including neomycin, ampicillin, metronidazole: 200 mg/L, and vancomycin: 100 mg/L) was added to the drinking water of mice. After 2 weeks of treatment to deplete the microbiota, FMT was performed. The collected fresh feces from the IF group mice were then mixed with appropriate amounts of sterilized water, ground, and added to 32 ml of sterilized water. Then, the FMT mice began consuming water that was prepared from the fresh feces of the IF group mice. For the Mettl3 over-expression mice group, the lentivirus for mettl3 overexpression was injected along with the GBM-inducing lentivirus. For the Intermittent Fasting plus Methionine (Tp53-MET-AL) group, the mice underwent a fasting schedule as IF group. The water provided to these mice contained 400 mg/kg of DL-Methionine (Shanghai Wankang Biotechnology Co., Ltd). For the Intermittent Fasting plus entacapone (Cdkn2a-ENT-AL) group, the mice underwent a fasting regimen and received intraperitoneal injections of entacapone78, at a dosage of 10 mg/kg, administered once weekly.

Bioluminescence imaging
All tumor cells were transduced with a lentiviral construct coding for firefly luciferase. At the terminal stage of the experiment, Brain tumor size was monitored by in vivo luciferase assay, by intraperitoneal injection of 15 mg/ml of Beyotime D-Luciferin potassium salt, and detecting brain luminescence with PerkinElmer IVIS Lumina XRMS (PerkinElmer Corporation, USA). Following image acquisition, the radiance values (photons) were obtained from the selected ROI areas for quantification.

Western blotting
The cells were lysed with RIPA lysate and centrifuged at 16,000 × g for 15 min at 4°C. The supernatants were collected, and total protein content was measured using the BCA assay. The mice brain tissues were lysed with RIPA lysate (P0013) and then further disruption by using a homogenizer, finally centrifuged to collect the supernatants. Lysates were separated with 10% SDS-PAGE, transferred to membrane filters, and subjected to immunoblotting using anti-TGF-β2 (1:1000, Proteintech, Cat#19999-1-AP), anti-METTL3 (1:1000, Abcam, ab195352), anti-GAPDH (D16H11) XP® Rabbit mAb (1:1000, Cell Signaling, #5174), and anti-Goat anti-Rabbit IgG H&L (1:10000, Abcam, ab216773). Cell lines T98G (Serial: SCSP-5274) were obtained from the National Collection of Authenticated Cell Cultures (NCACC).

LC-MS/MS conditions
The levels of methionine and m6A levels were measured in the brain tissue of AL (n=5 samples) and intermittent fasting (n=5 samples) mice by liquid chromatograph-mass spectrometer (LC-MS). Pooled quality-control samples were intermittently injected to assess analytical stability. Approximately 100 mg of tissue was homogenized in liquid nitrogen, extracted with pre-chilled 80% methanol, vortexed, incubated on ice for 5 min, and centrifuged at 15,000 × g for 20 min at 4°C62. The supernatant was diluted to 53% methanol with LC-MS–grade water, re-centrifuged, and the clarified extract was used for LC-MS/MS measurement.

The LC-MS/MS analysis was performed using a Vanquish UHPLC system (Thermo Fisher, Germany) coupled with an Orbitrap Q ExactiveTM HF-X mass spectrometer (Thermo Fisher, Germany). Samples were injected onto a Hypersil Gold column (100 × 2.1 mm, 1.9 μm) using a 12-min linear gradient at a flow rate of 0.2 mL/min. The eluents for the positive and negative polarity modes were eluent A (0.1% FA in Water) and eluent B (Methanol). The solvent gradient was set as follows: 2% B, 1.5 min; 2–85% B, 3 min; 85-100% B, 10 min；100–2% B, 10.1 min；2% B, 12 min. Q ExactiveTM HF mass spectrometer was operated in positive/negative polarity mode with spray voltage of 3.5 kV, capillary temperature of 320°C, sheath gas flow rate of 35 psi and aux gas flow rate of 10 L/min, S-lens RF level of 60, Aux gas heater temperature of 350°C. The raw data files generated by LC-MS/MS, as analyzed in Metabolomics analysis section.

Hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining
Freshly dissected tissues were fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde, processed routinely, and embedded in paraffin. Sections were cut at a thickness of 4–5 μm. Deparaffinized and rehydrated sections were stained with hematoxylin, differentiated, and blued following standard protocols. Subsequently, sections were counterstained with eosin, dehydrated, cleared, and mounted with a synthetic resin.

## Authors' Response to Round 1

Response: Thanks for the insightful suggestion. We apologize for any lack of clarity in our original manuscript. Initially, we compared differences between intermittent fasting (IF) and ad libitum (AL) conditions within the TP53-mutant genotype and observed phenotypic improvement in TP53-mutant mice upon IF. To further investigate why IF is effective specifically in the TP53-mutant subtype of GBM, all experiments from Figure 1 onward focused exclusively in the Tp53-subtype genetic background. Since CDKN2A-deleted mice did not exhibit improvement after IF, they were not initially included as controls.
As recommended, we have now included a comparative analysis between CDKN2A-AL and CDKN2A-IF groups as a control to better delineate the IF response specific to TP53-mutant GBM. Differential gene expression analysis between CDKN2A- and TP53-IF groups identified 2,741 significantly dysregulated genes, including METTL3—a key regulator of m⁶A methylation—providing further support that METTL3-mediated m⁶A modification may underlie the efficacy of IF in GBM (SF3b, 3c). Additionally, enrichment analysis revealed significant involvement of the TGF-β signaling pathway (SF3d, 3e).
These new results reinforce that the transcriptomic changes induced by IF are specific to TP53-mutant tumors and are not universally present across genetic subtypes.

4. To confirm that intermittent fasting is microbiome-dependent experiments in ABX-treated and germ-free setting should be perform.
Response: We agree that demonstrating the microbiome-dependency of the IF effect is crucial. 1. Limited novelty: The connection between METTL3 and Glioblastoma (GBM) has been extensively reported in multiple studies (Oncogene. 2018;37:522-533; Cancer Lett. 2021;511:36-46; Genes. 2019;10:141; Front. Oncol. 2021;11:702983; Cancer Res. 2019;79:5785–5798; Genome Biol. 2021;22:51.).
Response: We sincerely appreciate the valuable comments. However, our primary innovation does not lie in reiterating the downstream role of METTL3 in glioblastoma (GBM), which has indeed been extensively characterized. Instead, the novelty of our study is in demonstrating that the upstream regulation of METTL3 is governed by a diet-sensitive, microbiota-mediated m6A axis, and that this process is modulated by patient-specific genetic backgrounds. This discovery not only provides a new dimension to the established link between METTL3 and GBM, but also offers a conceptual framework for exploring the role of METTL3 within the broader context of the gut–tumor axis across other malignancies. Thus, while previous studies—including those as early as 2018—have reported on METTL3 in GBM, our focus diverges substantially, as the mechanistic emphasis is shifted from the tumor-intrinsic function of METTL3 to its upstream dietary and microbial regulation, which represents a distinct and highly innovative contribution.
Even though the regulatory role of METTL3 in GBM was first reported as early as 2018, studies related this topic continue to emerge, including reports published as recently as 2025 [1]. This once again highlights the sustained, pivotal role of METTL3 in glioblastoma biology, while also underscoring the distinct focus of each individual study.

Bioinformatic analyses initially helped us narrow the range of candidate pathways, including the MAPK-ERK, TGF-β, and HIF-1 pathways (F1h). At the outset, we did not know which pathway would be most critical. We therefore systematically evaluated them in turn [1,2]. First, when we examined the MAPK pathway, we observed no significant changes in either protein levels or phosphorylation status before and after IF treatment, and consequently did not pursue this pathway further. These negative results were omitted from the main text for clarity but informed the refinement of our study.

This study was conducted over a six-year period. Guided by bioinformatic analyses, we systematically evaluated several candidate pathways. All but the METTL3-TGF-β axis produced negative results. This divergence results in differential activation states of the TGF-β pathway, which ultimately drives the observed genotype-specific phenotypic responses.
9. More than 40 methyl transfers from S-adenosylmethionine (SAM) are known to occur to various substrates such as nucleic acids, proteins, lipids, and secondary metabolites. It is unclear why the authors focused specifically on m6A.
Response: We focused on m6A because an a priori survey of alternative SAM-dependent methylation pathways did not yield convincing candidates, whereas multiple independent lines of evidence converged on RNA m6A.
Specifically, global DNA methylation in GBM mouse brains before and after intermittent fasting (IF) was assessed using a Global DNA Methylation Assay kit, which showed no significant change (P = 0.82), arguing against DNA methylation as a major regulatory mechanism (a).
In parallel, histone methylation was profiled by sequencing, which revealed differential signals near BCAM, CEP170, SAMM50, and VPS33B; however, literature review and prognostic analyses indicated that these alterations had limited relevance to GBM biology (b, c). By contrast, unbiased RNA-seq after IF highlighted significant modulation of the m6A writer METTL3, which led us to perform targeted m6A-seq. These data confirmed reproducible remodeling of m6A marks post-IF, and functional perturbation experiments demonstrated that METTL3/m6A was necessary for the IF-associated phenotypes. Thus, our emphasis on m6A is data-driven: among the many SAM-dependent methylation reactions, only the m6A pathway consistently linked expression changes, epitranscriptomic remodeling, and functional impact under IF.

12. It is not unclear how IF treatment leads to a decrease in methionine-related gut microbial species.
Response: The gut microbiota is a highly complex ecosystem, comprising more than 5,000 species. In the colon of a 70-kg “reference man,” the total number of bacteria is estimated at approximately 3.8 × 1013. These microbial species also engage in intricate interactions with one another. Intermittent fasting (IF) reshapes this intestinal ecosystem through repeated substrate deprivation and ecological filtering, selectively constraining methionine-related microbial pathways and taxa [1]. Diet–microbiome studies have demonstrated that microbial methionine and sulfur metabolism is strongly substrate-driven [2]. Consistently, both IF and fasting-mimicking interventions remodel gut microbial composition and function in humans and mice. Together with our own antibiotic/FMT and rescue experiments, these findings support a model in which IF reduces the abundance of methionine-related microbes and methionine availability, thereby modulating METTL3-dependent m6A regulation and downstream TGFB2 expression.

Reviewer #3 (Remarks to the Author):
Reviewer Summary: In this manuscript, the authors examine the effect of intermittent fasting on the pathogenesis of GBM, stratified into groups driven by loss of TP53 and those with loss of CDKN2A. The authors found that IF only affected mice with tumors bearing TP53 deletion, which they found correlated with loss of methionine levels in tumor tissue. They found that this loss of methionine correlated to a loss of m6A, which they hypothesize leads to a reduction in TGFB signaling through METTL3.
The experiments performed in the study generally support the notion that intermittent fasting may regulate the gut microbiota and influence metabolism in orthotopic GBM in vivo. The methodology is sound and well described. The strengths of the manuscript are the mouse models used, the use of multiple omics platforms to measure gene- and metabolite-level data in tumor tissue, and rescue experiments to show the effects of methionine supplementation and entacapone in reversing the benefit of IF.
There are a few weaknesses in the manuscript.
First, the mechanistic link between IF and METTL3’s effect on TGFB is unclear from these studies. The authors do not provide evidence for how IF specifically influences METTL3, other than stating that TGFB likely has a reduction in m6A in IF mice. Further experimentation would help strengthen the link between IF and TGFB’s effects on tumor growth in their models. Specifically, it would be useful to show the effects of METTL3 knockout in AL mice and METTL3 overexpression in IF mice.
Response: Our data suggest that IF influences METTL3 through remodeling of the gut microbiota. Specifically, IF alters microbial composition, leading to a reduced abundance of methionine-producing bacteria. This reduction in methionine subsequently affects METTL3-mediated m6A regulation. Importantly, TGFB2 is one of the downstream targets of METTL3-dependent m6A modification.
As recommended, we have now included mice injected with STM2457 (METTL3 inhibitor, imitating METTL3 knockout) but ad libitum diet group, and mice with METTL3 overexpression and IF group. The results demonstrated that METTL3 inhibition even AL (Tp53-STM2457-AL) in Tp53 GBM mice groups slowed tumor growth (F5a, 5b, 5c) and significantly improved prognosis (F5d), but no significance in METTL3 overexpression even IF group (Tp53-M3OE-IF). Concurrently, we observed significant differences in the SAM and methionine levels in feces and serum (F5e, 5f, 5g, 5h), m6A levels (Figure 5i), and protein levels of TGFB2 and METTL3 (Figure 5j, 5k, 5l). Therefore, STM2457 injected in AL treated mice and METTL3 overexpression in IF-treated mice indicated that the tumor-suppressive effect of IF requires METTL3-mediated regulation of TGFB2.
Additionally, our fluorescence imaging data and protein-level analyses of TGFB2 and METTL3 provide consistent evidence supporting this pathway (F5j, 5k 5l). Together, these repeated rescue experiments strongly support the mechanistic link we propose.

Reviewer #4 (Remarks to the Author):
Lin et al. tried to link the genotype-specific tumor-inibiting effects of intermittent fasting (IF) on glioma development. However, a lack of experimental rigor, statistic testing, and key comparision across different genotypes makes their argument hardly convincing.
The experiments throughout lack a critical control group, Cdkn2a-mutant gliomas. IF should have similar effects on these mice, yet it is hard to explain why they are not nearly as responsive as Trp53-mutant mice.
Response: We feel great thanks for your professional review work.
In transcriptomics, we have now included a comparative analysis between CDKN2A-AL and CDKN2A-IF groups as a control to better delineate the IF response specific to TP53-mutant GBM. Differential gene expression analysis between CDKN2A- and TP53-IF groups identified 2,741 significantly dysregulated genes, including METTL3—a key regulator of m⁶A methylation—providing further support that METTL3-mediated m⁶A modification may underlie the efficacy of IF in GBM (SF2b, 2c). Additionally, enrichment analysis revealed significant involvement of the TGF-β signaling pathway (SF2d, 2e). These new results reinforce that the transcriptomic changes induced by IF are specific to TP53-mutant tumors and are not universally present across genetic subtypes.
In addition, we have performed metagenomic analysis comparing the gut microbiota of AL- and IF-treated CDKN2A and TP53 GBM mice (F4a, SF6a). Principal coordinate analysis (PCoA) and stacked bar plots at the phylum and class levels reveal distinct microbial community structures between these groups (F4a, 4b, 4c, SF6b, 6c). Additionally, LefSe analysis comparing CDKN2A-AL and CDKN2A-IF identified Alistipes as a genus enriched in the AL group (SF6e).
Meanwhile, in the fecal microbiota transplantation experiment from IF mice, Cdkn2a mice treated with AL and IF also be added as the control group. We found that CDKN2A mice did not show improvement in GBM after fecal transplantation (SF8a, 8c, 8c, 9d), further confirming that the CDKN2A phenotype is no response. However, we found that the levels of SAM and methionine in the feces and serum of in the CDKN2A-IF and the CDKN2A-FMT-AL mice groups were significantly decreased (SF8h, 8i, 8j ,8k), indicating that the reduction of SAM and methionine levels caused by IF is also effective in the CDKN2A phenotype.
Importantly, in our previous analyses, we observed that Tp53-mutated and Cdkn2a-deleted subtypes exhibit distinct genomic backgrounds and transcriptomic profiles. Due to the inherent complexity of human regulatory networks and ethical constraints, precise genetic manipulations-as performed in prokaryotic systems-are not feasible in human patients. To examine the potential differential effects of intermittent fasting, methionine restriction, and TGF-β signaling between these two GBM subtypes, we conducted comparative transcriptomic analysis.
Differential expression analysis revealed significant dysregulation of the TGF-β signaling pathway between TP53- and CDKN2A-patient groups [1] (SF2a, 2b). Specifically, Tp53-mutated tumors demonstrated reduced basal TGF-β pathway activity. This divergence in TGF-β activation suggests a subtype-specific mechanism underlying the differential response to METTL3-mediated m6A modification within the TGF-β pathway, ultimately contributing to the distinct phenotypic outcomes observed.
Collectively, these findings support a model in which the IF-methionine-TGF-β axis operates in a genotype-dependent manner in GBM, providing a mechanistic basis for subtype-specific vulnerabilities.

Kras overexpressing/mutation is uncommon in human GBMs, making these GBM models less relevant to human disease, which should be acknowledged.
Response: Thank you for your comments. Although mutations in the RAS gene itself are rare, alterations in the RTK/RAS pathway are detected in approximately 88% of glioblastoma (GBM) patients, and RAS occupies a central position within this pathway, regulating even PI3K [1] (see the 2008 TCGA landmark study entitled “Comprehensive genomic characterization defines human glioblastoma genes and core pathways”; Figure 5 of that paper provides a clear overview of the core pathways in GBM). Thus, dysregulation of the RAS pathway is a critical determinant for modeling clinical phenotypes of GBM. However, since it is not feasible to manipulate all genes within the RAS pathway, we focused on mutations in the central RAS gene itself to better recapitulate the clinical state of patients. Development of a novel mouse glioma model using lentiviral vectors
The same study also identified TP53 and CDKN2A as two additional core pathways. The TP53 pathway regulates senescence and apoptosis in downstream cells, whereas the CDKN2A pathway modulates G1/S phase progression. This differential regulatory mechanism may explain the distinct responses of these two pathways to TGFB2. Therefore, we suggest that this classification scheme for GBM deserves greater recognition.

Response: We thank the reviewer for this insightful comment. We agree that the original wording may have overemphasized the clinical recognition of the TP53- and CDKN2A-based classification. We have therefore revised the text to more accurately reflect the current state of the field. The TP53 and RB (in which CDKN2A is a key component) pathways are indeed among the three core pathways definitively altered in the vast majority of glioblastomas, as established by the foundational TCGA study [1]. While this pathway-based framework is profoundly influential for understanding disease biology, we acknowledge that it is not currently a primary method for clinical stratification, which more commonly incorporates markers like IDH mutation and MGMT promoter status. Our intention is to highlight the mechanistic importance of these pathways and suggest that their role in defining disease subtypes deserves further investigation, not to present them as a standalone clinical classification system.
Furthermore, in accordance with the reviewer's suggestion, we have removed the speculative statement regarding the decrease in excitatory neurons observed in scRNA-seq data, as its interpretation is indeed complex and not directly relevant to the central claims of our study.
Reference
[1] Cancer Genome Atlas Research Network. Comprehensive genomic characterization defines human glioblastoma genes and core pathways. Nature. 2008 Oct 23;455(7216):1061-8.
